Question: How come Lazarus - Free Pascal is almost never mentioned in 'programming' topics?

I don’t really know why but my feeling is just how badly Borland/Inprise did things. Back in around 1995, and remember this is just my feeling, other countries had different experience perhaps. This was well before C#. Java had basically failed at GUI App development but not for lack of trying. They really did try to fix things but they just made more and more technologies to do this and nothing got done and people did not know what to pick. This was basically open season and anything could become the next great thing. We had Visual C++ and Delphi competing. Universities I knew taught Pascal for the early computer science classes and C++ for later projects, more science-y. But Pascal was really popular and Visual C++ wasn’t really the “Visual” that people expected like Visual Basic, far far from it and it took a lot of work to get a GUI going. When you started a fresh clean empty Delphi project, you had a GUI window ready with About box and all. Just add some fields, buttons and you can program. Unlike Visual Basic, you had the complete source code visible and you could do anything you wanted, easily. The price was even amazing, just $99 for a smaller version, it was the same Delphi as the much more expensive one Delphi Pro was, you just did not get all the tools to work with databases and you did not get a source control, small stuff. It was quickly gaining ground and could become the biggest thing ever. I was a harden Delphi developer. Nothing else mattered as far as I was concerned. I just got the small version, that came with a lot of books and tutorials, you name it. I found some MySQL components and I was off and running, though I mostly used a database called Paradox. But some “money” people bought Borland, and it went down like Titanic and Pascal kind of vanished. Now now, Delphi still exists but it hasn’t really changed much except the price is ridiculously high. I just think that since the main developer behind Delphi and Turbo Pascal before that, Anders Hejlsberg, went to Microsoft and created C# and a little later he made Typescript among others. Without someone pushing Pascal as an alternative, it simply became a small player in the world. This also makes interest in FreePascal quite minimal, which in turn reduces interest that might be there for FreePascal. Even someone who was likely to tattoo themselves with Pascal simply gave up and I moved along. Last time I touched Delphi was in 2000, most people who use Delphi today are most often someone who had apps before 2000 and continues to use Delphi. I can’t comment on the status of Delphi, it might very well have improved greatly but it simply isn’t on my radar. Which is a shame. Like I use 2 slices of cheese on toast, I only need to weigh it once, I know what it is now and just pick it from a list. Learn to cook. I am telling you, homemade food is so much better and it isn’t filled with all sorts of chemicals to make the food “fresh” for a long time. Making a stew takes like no time, chicken stick, cut of meat, some vegetables. Spices. It is easy. Add some rice, not as much as you would like. Then you need to monitor your eating. Don’t eat more than you can. If you do, just write it down. Great apps like Loose it are very good at helping you. It knows amazing amounts of basically all foods around. Just weight it first. Learn what 200 gr. of yogurt looks like. Once you feel comfortable, you just pick the food from a list of known foods. Here is the kicker, and this is why most people quit. They stop seeing results. I know just how I sound, because I have heard this myself for 30 years. YOU don’t see results because you see yourself every day. The results are small every time. But you have friends you have not seen in 6 months and they change often drastically. A friend mine who was seriously overweight, did not see him for a year, he kind of looks like Michael Phelps today. He admits he has trouble seeing results but he is literally half the man he used to be, and that is good. All he changed is quit energy drinks (Red Bull, Monster and such) and started to bike some, not much, just some. As he got more energy, he biked more. Nothing planned. But he almost does not drink alcohol anymore, just doesn’t want it. Rambling start I decided just last week to quit energy drinks. I did take my eating seriously for the last year but I gained weight, crept up. I did register all my eating, it wasn’t excessive. Then like 4–5 months ago, I started to sweat like crazy. I could take my hand and push sweat off my head and it would drip down like rain after just a little walk. I wasn’t that fat, I had been active, walking, playing discgolf. This did not fit. So, my poor baby sister got a call. I could not and dared not play discgolf with friends. She is a doctor by the way. We went over everything. Good thing I am a stickler to writing down everything, electric scale since 2011, every day. Apple watch, Android watch, never skip a beat. Always clock in everything, heart rate and you name it. Now, my energy drinks drinking was just a can in the morning, sometimes two but never after lunch, never ever. I figured the caffeine would be under control. She talked to me like a little kid, and I allowed her because I felt stupid. I never suspected the energy drinks. So, I quit cold turkey. It wasn’t hard as I just started to drink a little coffee instead, black. One cup in the morning. I am just quitting energy drinks. In 3–4 days, my heartbeat average is 10 lower than it has been for 6 months. My weight is dropping like my stock portfolio, good for the weight, not for the portfolio. My internal system is just more relaxed, I sleep better (watch monitors my sleep). I swear, everything is better. Now, just 7–8 days later, I went on a monster course in discgolf, lot of hiking, no sweat. WTF!!!! Rambling over. Small things matter. Here is what I would do. Buy a nice shirt, nothing overly expensive. Just one that looks good, perhaps slim fit. Buy it in Large or X-Large. Something that you can put on but you can’t button it. Once a month, or week, measure how far it is. I am telling you, this works. This is where you see progress. Also, keep your favorite pants. Get into it. Now relax, pull it in the button above the zipper. Measure how far it goes from your body. These things take time. There is no shortcut. If you go crazy into exercise, run, bike and lift weights like every day, you will injure yourself and you will quit. Expect to see and witness results in 4 months. Don’t have a cheat day, but don’t live like a Monk either. Eat food, the food you like. Skip ice cream, fried food. You won’t miss it after a while. Take a baked potato. Bake it at home. Loose it, the App, both on Android and iPhone. It allows you to be nicer to yourself on weekends. When picking what to eat, ask the app for calories. Stay away from like Pasta salad, unless you make it, you never know just how much sugar is in it, unless it is on the box. So what if you have a bad day. so what if you gain weight, especially when you are starting. Don’t worry about it. Don’t overly blame yourself. Remember, if you eat bread, you will carry water, you can gain a little weight. Rice? You gain some water weight, you will pee it in a day or two. Too much salt one day? No worries. Do things that you can see yourself doing forever. It is like, how do you get a black belt in martial arts sport? Just show up, do something every day. It is all about showing up. It takes at least 7 years to get black belt. You did not gain the weight in 3 months, don’t expect to remove it in 3 months. Fix what is wrong. Need beer? Buy zero caloric beer or close to it, light this, no carb beer. Doesn’t taste as good, but still is good. Gin and tonic? How about Gin and soda water? It is actually even better than tonic. Put some thought into it. One last thing. This is a bit wasteful, but still, it works. If you can’t cook, don’t have the place or something. You always eat out. Well, write down everything you eat, every day for 3–4 weeks. Now, eat the same food, but just half, and throw it away. I know. Throw it away. It works. Skip the fries. Question: What is the minimum number of patrons for a theater to start a movie? If there's just two seats filled, would there be refunds?
Answer: I love watching movies so much, that when I was younger it was hurting my economy. When I figured out that if you work as a projectionist, you can see movies for free when you are not working. A total win win situation. When I was showing, we had film. Usually a movie would come in 6 to 9 parts of film like this I would take them and I would tape them together, no, seriously, tape them. You would put one film on one end, then the other on the other end, fine tune it with the knob on the front. You don’t want it to have a space, then the whole move is out of place, or even a bright line above, no one wants that. Not too close either, that could open up the lid keeping the film “flapping” and cause havock. In the very old days it could burn down the theater as back then they were highly flammable. But you needed to either put the film together, half and half like this Not me, but good looking fellow. Or if you planned on showing this film often, this is what you had When you were no longer showing the movie, you would track the film, through the projector and onto the bottom reel. But you had to stop the movie exactly where the end of one reel is, exactly. More than 3–4 reels don’t fit on that holster and you are absolutely not allowed to take two intermissions, no way, no how. How can you tell if the film reel is about to finish? You see that black dot. Usually they are not that noticeable. They appear for a fraction of a second, and then appear again in 10 seconds which gives you time when the first one appears to turn on the lights, lower the sound, turn on the radio or music and stop the projector. Then you take scissors, no, not some special movie scissors but Find the frame where you glued everything together, and cut, often you could just use a quick hand movement, sometimes not. So. You see, there is a lot that goes into showing a movie. A lot of work. And once the movie has started, you have to at least show half of it, but if you have the platter, you simply have to show the complete movie, you can’t do anything otherwise, that film has to go from A to B, in order to be shown again. If the film f.ex. falls off the plate and onto the floor, you have kilometers of film that is very inflexible, very twisty and annoying. Behaves in its own way. I could say annoying but it is much worse than that. So. If you started the movie at the dot, say 21:00, you simply finish the movie. You and the people working there might get popcorn and watch it. You know where the dots are, so you work your magic if you need to. If you did not start the movie, you were good to do whatever. But people do come late, so if you suspect that, you have to start the movie, a 90 minute movie will run like 100 minutes, and it has to go from A to B. It is way easier with the new downloadable movies. You can simply press stop and that is it. If we managed to close ticket sales, we would just leave everything for that showing. But if you have many rooms, you just play it.

Question: Why do programmers read books on how to program rather than watch tutorials?
Answer: I am not a young programmer. I am willing to go with that. When I was starting out, there were no videos, no internet. All you had were books. Schools also use books. But one reason to prefer books over videos is basically the book is more organized, it delves deeper and can explain so much more and it takes you 2 minutes to read a page, give or take. A video is 30 minutes, minimum if it is of any value (except for the 100 second videos by Fireship, they are spectacular). Video is all about subscribing, selling more expensive videos, introduction and stuff you don’t need. If you ask my wife, I have tens of thousands of programming books, fortunately most of them are e-books which my wife does not know about. But I have a lot, could be 100, could be more. I have not read them all, not even close. I own books that are 1000 pages but I only bought them for a part of one chapter. I just might have needed that part, then and there, just that time. But these books come in handy all the time. Even for completely unrelated matters. One book on Java might have a data structure I need for a Python project. An iPhone book has a great chapter on OpenGL. A Mac book of just 100 pages has by far the best chapter on Core Data of all books, including books just on Core data, and it does Core Data in 5–6 pages. I go through the index and chapters of most of my books all the time. I pretty much know where to look. It is easy. My e-books are way easier. I have a giant folder on a NAS that is called books. I simply search for a topic and Spotlight gives me what I want. Some of the books are Epub which means I really can’t search all that well, but I have command line tools because all the text in the books is a text file. It is a mixed bag. But I do love videos. Most of the people I subscribe to on Youtue and Instagram are programmers. But I see a lot of them going down a rabbit hole of self help and leaving, many have stopped. Quality is not guaranteed. Lets take one of the guys I subscribe to, completely random. Tim Corey from IamTimCorey. He makes amazing videos. He is a world renowned C# developer. He also does Python and other programming. This is where books come in strong. Each chapter can build on prior chapters but a given chapter is just about this thing you want. It is easier, faster and more to the point. Today, I will admit. I run my own AI at home, no I did not make it, I just installed it, llama. I use that more often than I will admit to teach me some things, if it fails, I use ChatGPT a lot as well. I can just say, life is a lot easier today than it was in 1995 when you had built in help inside your editor like Turbo Pascal, and that was all you had. Question: What features of VB6 are particularly challenging to migrate to modern frameworks?
Answer: VB6 was abandoned in 2008, that is 16 years ago, just for clarity. I had to check to see how old this question was, weird it was made in 2024. If the tool is still in use, that is simply astounding but all such apps should have died a decade ago. There isn’t one feature of VB6 that makes it difficult to “migrate” over to a new platform. First and foremost, VB6 is an enclosed tool. You program a button directly, you program a textfield directly. You don’t make your model objects. You basically program inside your app. All your code which you can still open in any text editor use useless, let me rephrase this, every single line of code is useless except for reading it to figure out what is happening. No platform* can use this code. So, your complete source code is useless. You usually opted for tools that directly connected to a database, so you have these arrows to go back and forth with your database, when you are entering in data, you are directly putting data into a database. It was an amazing tool for simple apps and many of them were quite useful. I honestly think that MS made a mistake here, there is a market for such very low barrier tool. But basically, the problem is that you need to re-make the application in much more complicated environments. You need to use completely different tools, different languages, different GUI tools and just everything. You saw my * above, well, there is a tool like it, but gives you everything else as well. It allows you to make simple “form” apps, but also grows with your talent. It is completely OOP (object oriented programming). You can make easily model objects, connect to any database, write your own SQL if you will. It has Interfaces, low level access to native API and best of all, it compiles down to native code. No slow runtimes. It is fast, it is great. It used to be called RealStudio which is a name I much more prefer than what it is called today, XOJO (Cross-platform App Development Tool ). Naming isn’t everything and this tool has been around with the same owners for at least 25 years and isn’t going anywhere. Their economy is strong and people on the forums are helpful to a fault (basically too helpful). There used to be a tool to read in a VB6 project into XOJO, I simply don’t know how far that get’s you but I think you should get pretty far. At least you would not need to rewrite everything. I love this tool even though I don’t use it today. I made tons of money on it, made shareware apps that paid for many computers, large screens and so forth. If you are moving from VB6, Xojo is your tool. For the last decade and then some, I have written code in all sorts of languages. I love C#, I love their tools and everything. Well, everything BUT writing GUI tools. I dislike writing desktop Apps in C#. It is simply way more complicated than it has to be. This is where Xojo comes in strong. It is precisely the tool you need to write desktop apps. I would not use it to write Web apps, except if it had minimal amount of users and came as an extra to an app I already had written in Xojo, then it is absolutely amazing. Delphi is another tool I would suggest, it is Pascal but quite powerful. But as far as I know, it has been decades since I last used it, it hasn’t really changed much, if anything. It is basically the same tool but it costs insane amounts of money. But it is still there, that is something VB6 is isn’t. If I was tasked with taking a VB6 app and make it modern. I would fight tooth and nail to make it a web app. Chances are great it is already a client server thing. Making it into a web app should not take long. Most VB6 apps were small. If that would fail, I would absolutely use Xojo. And frankly if I could not get that through, I would walk away from the project, no, I would run. It is doomed to be a failure and you are the one everyone will blame for the failure, not the ones who made the decisions. Now, if you can get it into a web app. Use whatever tool you know. Even PHP or go with Ruby on rails, Django to name two. Something that get’s you there quickly. If you have more budget, make it in C# for example and use Razor pages (not Blazor, it is a deep well where you get stuck in overly complicated things). If you get a bit more budget, perhaps make the front end in a nice Javascript like react or vue. Have fun. If there is a budget, I might be interested in such a project, but I would have to have something to say about it :)

Question: What is the use of object-oriented database?
Answer: Now, take this with a grain of salt. I also struggle a bit with OO databases. But as far as I can tell, it gives you 1 to 1 relations to your objects in your app. So you can take a huge object tree and just call save and it saves and updates your tree. It also allows you to create base tables and then inherit them for more complicated objects. Now, this isn’t, in my opinion, a NoSQL thing like MongoDB. But I think in all fairness that OO database is more of a teaching tool, something students use to learn from. It can also be used with things like Sharepoint, Lotus Notes and other business tools where non programmers might do a lot of work and this makes it easier to link data and views. But as a programmer, for over 30 years. Outside of just curiosity, the use of OO database simply has never ever come up. Even the OO features in Postgres where you can inherit table structure and it does some magic behind the scenes, I have never seen it used outside of tutorials. From my point of view, especially with Databases, they have to be reliable. Under no circumstances should you be able to destroy everything unless you use specific commands to do so. Yes I am fully away that forgetting a WHERE clause in DELETE from statement is dangerous. But what if you have an OO database and you radically change the root object, change the fields and even values from strings to numbers and cases like that. I think there are probably business tools that make use of it, some report tools. But if you have programmers working for you, use them and forget all those “no code” tools. An ORM (Object relational mapper) is much more likely to succeed.

Question: Is asynchronous programming achieved by using multiple threads?
Answer: It could be. Like Elixir, DotNet, Go and such. They use all sorts of tricks that is outside of your controls. They might run on a different core but it is not guaranteed. Usually asynchronous is simply so called event loop. It is basically just an endless loop that has a list of tasks that need to be done. When you add a task by using async calls, you are added into the list. You get a promise back which keeps the status of your request. Behind the scenes there is a scheduler. It just goes over your task list and asks the promiser if they are done, if done it returns your data else it goes next in line and vice verse. If this is for example a restful API, each query it gets is also sent to the list or queue. The scheduler then simply gives each task a chance to run for a while, then it goes to the next one and that one runs for a while. So and so on. It usually runs on a single core, doing one thing at a time. This is also why if you ask for 5 things to be done, it finishes out of order. If you don’t call async, it will run everything in the sequence it got the work. But while it is running, everything else is blocked, meaning if you run a large task this way, write gigabytes to the storage. Nothing else runs until it is finished. That is called blocking call and should mostly not be used or called, but there are circumstances where it is needed. JavaScript and Node are guaranteed to run only on one core doing one thing at a time. You can use libraries which use more cores, but then you really should know what you are doing, locks, semaphores and all sorts of edge cases.

Why did he point to that specific project, mistake, he accidentally copy pasted the github url on that project, and in that project he was doing cool things but the code was a complete mess, it was an autocomplete mistake. Question: Which developers are expensive to hire? Ruby on Rails, Php or Python? Why?
Answer: This is my experience. You seldomly pay for specific language or framework skills. Of course if you need a Python developer, it does not matter how much the Ruby developer costs. If you need Wordpress developer or Drupal, then a simple PHP developer would not be the right match, you want experience. Now. Even a good Wordpress developer would always take a few days to get started and get all the requirements in. You could hire any PHP developer who is not experienced and negotiate a much lower rate. That is quite popular as well. Back when I was doing iOS development in Objective C, you would have needed to pay quite a high fee for me. But I would easily cut 50% or even a little more for other projects I wasn’t as familiar with, say Ruby on Rails. Quite often I take in requirements and give you an estimate on the total price or even negotiate on the total price, one lump sum, paid in 3 stages or so, depending on the length of the project. Despite my willingness to charge very little, I need to eat and pay bills, so I have a base minimum fee and I also have a high rate for shorter projects where I am quite experienced and warm in. When I say warm, I mean it is similar to projects I have done lately. I could do any Python related project and get started right away, but my muscle and brain memory is not loaded, not warm. My solution for such is both to charge less and even just charge 4–5 hours for 8 hours worked if I feel I have not delivered much in the beginning. Later in the project, you might not see any progress on anything but I am working my ass off, you just don’t see it, common thing that pisses off managers and developers. But there are ways to see progress. Outside of his answer. My advice is not to look at price for specific languages. Most of the work is in database management, user rights, front end pixel pushing. Find out what you need. If you want a developer to write a specific app for you, consider how hard it is to hire the next person to do changes, the next version. Unless you are hiring the developer full time, they might not be available when you need them. I see this all the time that companies paint them in a corner and need to abandon pretty nice apps because they either can’t find anyone or think they are too expensive. Most markets, areas and places have usually strong favorable tech stacks. Some areas are high on Ruby or Python while other places are DotNet through and through. This could limit you quite a lot, often this is tied with what Universities nearby teach and availability of public courses. Make sure you know some of the lingo, some of what goes into making the app or get a friend who knows. Nothing is more infuriating when projects take much longer time than anticipated. Also keep in mind that whenever you suggest a small change, outside of what was agreed on, will add more time. Even if YOU think it should be 10 minutes. You need often a major cleaning to add a small item. The item takes perhaps a few hours but it can take much longer to accommodate it, or you stopped work in other areas which are then not done on time and delay other things that rely on it. Here is my final advice on the issue. Make sure you hire a developer who is honest with you and you need to be honest as well. Let’s start with you. You need to tell them everything, when you plan on launching, what budget you are dealing with, where you will host the app, what you expect to happen in what timeframe. Everyone is clear that things can take less time but more often you need to add a little wiggle room. Don’t expect to go live next week. A little pressure helps but it can also have the opposite effect. Make sure you tell them they check in code every day, at end of every day, no exceptions, on your server where they are not admins. Failure to check in code, even if it doesn’t work means penalties. Work in short rounds with clear project goals, no step should take more than 2 days, best is to keep it smaller. You also need to be clear on payments. When certain steps are reached, you pay. When steps are not finished, partial payment is paid, as negotiated. You also must be clear if you are on a fixed budget, that a certain sum is the total max for this work, you also must hold back any changes to any plan. Remember, you are on the same team, communicate. The developer must know this. The developer should feel comfortable to tell you that some stupid bug took way longer than he thought because he misspelled a controller name as UserControlcontroller, which the system was happy with but nothing worked and no code suggestions gave anything away. Shit happens. They need to be honest with how things are going even if it looks bad. I have seen projects seemingly go from bad to worse quickly just to get finished very shortly afterwards with huge success. That is more common than one would expect. No yelling what so ever. You are not talking to a dog who chewed your expensive sofa. This is a professional, you are a professional. Behave like one, when in doubt you both have lawyers or some other means where both parties know what is happening. Contracts are always great. Remember, they are not there for two friends to have fun and drink beer. They are there when things go bad. Contracts are the only thing that is usable in court, emails, sms and verbal things only work if both parties are clear on the meaning. Good luck with this. You pay for experience. It is always good to get a technical person you know to get things going, even if it is just a few hours.

Question: What is an SQL function?
Answer: A function is a piece of program that gives you results, some answer. That is the normal meaning of a function. Of course you can have void functions, which return nothing but still. Many programming languages like Pascal and other variants of Pascal had a requirement that function returns something and gave you procedures for “functions” that returned nothing. SQL function is an SQL Query that usually takes in parameters like date_to and date_from, last name and such. It then executes the query and gives you the results. This is quite common when you have the same query or similar ones running in many places, then you don’t need to keep many copies of the query, you store it in a function, which can be called from wherever. Many relational databases give you an option to store function inside itself, so you can call a function with either some execute call or SELECT call. Many queries rely on built in functions, like MATH functions, SELECT SUM(price) WHERE order_id=1234; There SUM is a function, where it is really just a query which adds the results up and just gives you that answer. Other popular MATH functions are ABS which always gives you a positive number, SELECT ABS(-100), ABS(100) …. gives you two fields of 100 Functions are there to make your life easier. Like taking a date which is a string ‘2024–08–12’ and be able to convert it to a date which you can then get all transactions made after four o’clock on that date.

Anyway, I could buy ebooks, print them at work, 300–600 pages, both sides in what felt like a few minutes. The time it took me to walk to the printer, was like the time it took to finish, not exactly but close. The company looked so cool. I was located on a different floor than my division I worked in, I was in one project which was a doozy. Now bear in mind, I had lived like 5–6 years in Norway, I did not know my left from my right as I had mostly been at work the whole time. So, working for some official government agency told me nothing. But my first 2 months were cool-ish. There were signs, all signs that I considered part of a “grown up company”. Yeah, more meetings. Even if there were pre-meetings, meetings, after meetings and then some sort of a summary meeting. Yes the project had 4 highly competitive companies each doing their part and blaming each other for being late, we had 5–6 contract project managers. We had my division and myself. I had worked for SUN Microsystems itself, I had huge Unix background. Here I was dealing with a SUN sales person who sat on both sides of the table trying to get us to use brand new cool computers with Niagara CPU from SUN, which cost the whites of your eyes. We are talking James Bond stuff here, seriously, evil layer inside a volcano. I could not be more serious, seriously. This was the coolest place I have even been inside. We are talking about guards everywhere, armed? I would actually think they had arms there, I don’t know. Ever felt like you were 2cm tall? It was in there. Everything was huge. I was in all sorts of meetings. People invited me to meetings because they felt lonely, that is the only conclusion I can think of. Then I went into my first meeting with the governmental agency, only to find out that they themselves already had gigantic server rooms. They had a lot of the biggest SUN servers money could buy. They knew a lot more about SUN and Solaris than I would ever do. In Norway, they knew a lot more about SUN than SUN in Norway did. They were experts, the finest and best I have seen since I left SUN. They were amazing. They could have run this new system all by themselves in one of these E10000 or E15000 they had, and they had a lot of them, seriously. You are looking at this wrong. Completely. Now, feel free to over complicate this as much as you want but here is the GIT 101. Git is amazing for solo developers, small teams and all the way up to enormous teams. You have a branch called Main or Master. It is a good idea that NO ONE can commit directly on that branch. You should only allow pull requests from Staging in there, no other branch. But if the project is small, then just use the next branch, Dev. Dev branch. It is the source of truth, kind of like your trunk. This is the latest code. Unless it is a very small project, you should normally not commit directly on Dev, no one. You should always branch from dev based on ticket or project. Call your branch like “bug/1124-missing-phonenumber”. The branching of bug/ feature/ fix/ and so forth is not needed as branches are deleted once they are merged. But if you are working on many branches at the same sprint / time, it is a good rule. Now, keep in mind, you can do this all completely locally with no internet connection. You then make a pull request from “bug/1124-missing-phonenumber” (or “T-1124-….”) into dev. This makes it possible for some other people to look over your code, code review. Code review is great, it keeps you from accidentally leaving passwords, tokens and other secrets in the code, it also helps to get rid of accidental logging. But once you are merged, and others working on other tickets, they can now pull the latest changes from Dev branch, it might hurt their code if they don’t like you added a field to the database. This is also a fantastic time to have a build server like Jenkins (completely free) to run tests on your code, including end to end tests, like do all database queries still work. Did you accidentally re-introduce old bugs? Is there something breaking? Then a build master, makes a pull request from Dev to Staging. Staging usually has real database, often a clone of production, no one should have access to that database directly of course except through code. Staging then runs all tests again with real production data, which is quite often weirder than any programmer can do on Dev. Some people add Test branch between with a Test database. It is up to your team to decide if external services should be mimicked, if you have full stack like Redis, cache servers to test or not. This makes it easy to do simpler tests on Dev and increased one on Test and then full stack test on Staging. Then things go into Main / Master and go to production. It is up to the team to decide when Dev goes into Test/Staging. But Thursdays are great for that, or Mondays. You should then make production ready on say Wednesday, you have some days to fix things that could come up. Now, for everything, any day is fine to do whatever. But please for the love of everything, never release into production on Friday, no matter what, even a small one liner. You never know what can and will happen. As Murphy says, if something can go wrong, it will. If you see some bad things happening once in a while on your computer, know that it will happen a lot on production. Final thoughts. I use the Main/Master -> Test -> Dev -> feature ranch on every project I do, no matter how small they are, if the project is large enough to use a version control, this is what I do. By doing this always, I always do it. That might sound stupid, but if you don’t touch a project for 3 week or 3 months, you forget everything. But if you always keep the same structure, you at least don’t need to remember that and it is in muscle memory. besides, it is a good practice to have good practice with your projects. It isn’t even hard work. And if you are out travelling, you just pull down latest changes and then after that, don’t worry about internet connections. Dev branches can have much simpler settings than a Test/Staging. You could even have SQLite database instead of a full blown SQL Server/Oracle, you can have very limited data, just enough to make tests work locally. The old way of working was dreadful at the time when there was nothing else. If you want to check out something super cool. Check out Fossil SCM. It is made by the ever great Dr. Richard Hipp, the maker of SQLite. The SQLite code is in Fossil. It is self hosting, as the server that shows up on sqlite . org, is Fossil itself. It has built in issue tracker, wiki pages and much much more. It works also without network and at the end of the day, everything is stored in a SQLite database, so is is quite robust. It works very similar to Git. I personally use Git but used Fossil for years. I am just to used to Git at work now.

Name: Trausti Thor Johannsson
Question: Is freelancing or full-time employment making the right choice as a Ruby on Rails developer?
Answer: I don’t know if I should start the negative first or positive …. Let’s see how I do. I love freelancing, best thing in the world. I have freelanced as an iPhone developer, web developer and system administration, kubernetes deployments and much more. There is like nothing better, seriously. The biggest downside of being a contractor is that you don’t have any friends at work, even on a long term project of over 6–10 months, you are not usually invited to company stuff like trips, celebration and such. Even though your boss is a complete ass hole (you are your boss in case of misunderstanding), I love being a freelance contractor. Before the real negative. Being a fulltime employee means you have co-workers, health insurance, days off, vacation and most companies have free drinks, coffee and even food but there are also massages, therapists, gym membership and I could go on. You usually get food and coffee if available. You get a paycheck at the end of the month, taxes paid, holiday pay put in correct place and so forth. Companies give you the equipment you need and such, as a contractor you often get company equipment but mostly you need to bring your own, which is usually great as I tend to buy better equipment than any company would get me. It is relatively stress free of being salaried employee, in my case, I have never less than 3 months on salary if I get laid off, sometimes it can be 6 months. You can look at this like playing frisbee golf as a professional. As an employee, you work on what the company tells you to, not always fun. As a contractor, you still work on what the company wants you to work on. You will use a lot of time doing billing. You need to make contracts of what is included like if they pay for lunch, expenses like travel and many other things you normally never consider. Most often, companies will just pay an hourly wage, not during lunch, no overtime and most often it is not required. You need to keep a journal over what it is that you do every day, because someone completely unrelated to your project will nitpick your hours every month or week. They never believe you are under reporting, which is something you will do. You need to keep every receipt, every receipt. I usually have a company, ltd or ehf or AB depending on the country. This protects me. You can always get sued for any number of things. Including the company you work for going under, you have unpaid bills and the new people who bought it or lawyers in charge of the bankruptcy will use their powers to get you to forfeit your bill, you are much easier to deal with than a large corporation. This is why you should get such an insurance eventually, talk to my lawyer is always the ace in the arm in such cases. A board member might take it upon themselves to sue you for your bills or just to be an ass hat. Even if the person in charge of the project is happy and stamps approval on everything, you might still get sued or called in again to defend your bills, this is why a journal is super important. You can’t do it the week after, you have forgotten. If you commit code, keep the commit id’s at least. Notion is a great tool for this. If you get sued, they can only go after the company, not you. They can never take your house. Same if your company goes bankrupt, it happens. You just lose what the company had, not your own money, house, car and such. If you bill using a VAT number and your ID, you are open up for losing everything. Never co-sign a company loan unless you have to, it is easier to bankrupt the company and start another one. You need to deal with tax office, accountants, business bureaus, follow up on payments and you need to do pay salary to yourself. Keep in mind that this way, you could be entitled to unemployment benefits if you run out of projects but you need to pay that extra, and usually you pay yourself bottom salary and the money accumulates in the company, both great ideas except if you need insurance, paid back sick days and such, you get the bottom salary. When you get a house loan, that is your salary. I hate the book keeping part, scanning receipts, talking to accountants. I just want to do the work. The middle ground is to get what I call a pimp. There are many companies out there that companies call on to find them contractors, you go through them. You bill them, not the company and you are forbidden to even contact the company for a year or two afterwards, you can’t accept another project from the company if they offer it, you go through the pimp. Usually you bill the pimp and the pimp has insurances and you will always get paid no matter what. You talk to the pimp if you are unhappy with things, like things moving slowly. Usually the pimp has 60–90 days before they pay your first bill. That isn’t bad, this means you get paid for 2–3 months after you finished the project and you get to find another project while getting paid, and if the pimp gets you another project, you are usually good to go. This way, you have much simpler billing practices and they are in much better situation to ask the client to pay for expenses if you need them, like traveling than you will ever be. But today, I am good as a salaried employee. My income is much more level. I miss having to “need to buy” new computers to get my tax rate down, costs reduce your taxes in certain cases. Then f.ex. in Sweden, you need to estimate how much you will earn every year and pay taxes on that, which means you pay taxes every months or two, for income you have not received. There are pluses and minuses on everything. I can’t say all my full time employments have been all that good. My contract work was almost all good but it is stressful to be between projects because I am never in between paying bills. One thing, try to do something on the side. Make some websites on things that people will read, get ad revenue. Help companies with setting up webstores and charge a little every month. Setup hosting servers and charge companies a fixed monthly sum. This will add up to perhaps a thousand or two a month if you are lucky, eventually. This could prevent you from ever having late payments on your own bills. This also pays for vacations, sick days and so forth. This even pays for you to go climbing in Greece, frisbee golf in Sweden, skiing in Norway. Just make sure you have some business there, like talk to someone about Rails. Make sure your company is always in plus. If you happen to own some money in there, you can get the company to expand into renting office space and you name it. Never dry up your company.

Question: How do programmers understand more million lines of code?
Answer: You don’t understand all the code by reading it. Not million lines. Usually, programs follow patterns, like there is a menu or events, which then triggers something. You then follow the code. Code is generally understandable. Like reading English in a way. You try to gather context and see where what happens. You will never just know all million lines but given a few days or weeks, you will ca know where you need to look for something. And here is a catch. I have been involved in very large code bases, you don’t read the whole code, ever. Even those that wrote most of it don’t remember most of it. What you do, usually when you fix a bug, you find the place where it happens. Sometimes it takes a debugger to find it, other times you might know a variable, class, call, function or a string to search for. But it isn’t hard to find the place where it happens. You should be able to do so in 30 minutes, max. When you add new features, it is often trickier. Then you usually follow how code is written there already. You will not introduce your own way of spacing, camel cases for variables or things like that. You try to follow patterns already established as best as you can. You usually find where other operations are happening which are close to where you need to be and add yours there. Usually that is easiest with regards to connecting everything and not needing to re-invent the wheel. Now. If this is some old software you are going to rewrite in a new language. This is much more involved than anything else. I will shorten this bit dramatically as this is a case for a book or two even. When you rewrite a service, completely, often in a different language or dramatically newer tools. You need to map things out. Think like a telephone operator in a way. You need to monitor the old system, find the inputs the system accepts and what it does to that information. If it is possible, it is good to write tests in the old system where you can mock things, like get an input, call the right functions and then keep the output. If that isn’t possible, gather a lot of inputs and collect all the outputs. Depending on how involved everything is, we could be talking about hundreds or thousands of examples, no need to test many copies of same inout and output. Then little by little, you write enough code in the new system to get the same inout and deliver the same output. This seems tedious and sometimes it feels like you are not moving at all. But usually this is fun, involving and satisfying. Looking at the old code and seeing all the ifs elses and buts. Your question is really good but it could use a little context. Many different types of answers for different scenarios. But if you are new and you have this project, don’t try to eat an elephant in one bite. These things take time. Usually you get projects and bug fixes, you just find similar code in the right place. Even after 5 years there could be 3/4 of the project you have never looked at. No one expects you to know a large project. Imagine a map of a country. Know where some interesting places are. The rest will just come to you. Most important is to adjust your style to the style of the project, even if it is stupid in your opinion, less effective or ugly. You will get pushback on every minor detail that is different. Tab vs spaces is a real thing.

Question: What are the steps to become good in C programming in a year with no programming experience?
Answer: First things to become great in anything. Be it martial arts, weight lifting, running, carpentry, electricity, house building, car repairs, painting and pretty much anything is to take the time it needs to learn things. It takes years to become a good programmer. It is quite different to make a game engine and then to write a financial app or salary calculator. Very different. You can learn C in just a few weeks. University will teach you some C and in a full year, you will be doing quite a lot with it, some even write programs that render images, that is, take in a description of circles, camera settings, lights, reflections and calculate this. But they don’t write such a renderer because they learnt C. They learn this because they ALSO learnt a lot of Math, Calculus and Physics. Under guidance and in group settings, they could make all these things come together and describe their problems in C. There is a huge difference in learning a language and being a programmer. When I was a kid, 12 year old kids wrote all sorts of games in BASIC, some even could learn a little assembly. But it took years to become good. Don’t let this discourage you. But you have no idea what programming is, of course you don’t know. You are under the assumption of learning a language and you can build anything. That is just far from the truth. That is like knowing how to hammer a nail in a plank of wood and think you can build a house, you can’t, not a house you can live in at least. Take the time it takes. Some people learn some aspects rights away and struggle elsewhere, others take some more time. Everyone is different. Now, people, don’t take this too literally. But languages are just tools to get the job done. It does not matter if you learn C, Java, C#, Erlang, Elixir, F#, Scala or anything else. It really does not make a difference. Just stick with it. Learn more. Once you can write a program that you use to write down information on stamps, cars, books or anything that is near and close to you, you can easily write such programs, just know that there is much more to it. Searching, sorting to just name two, going from first record down to last record isn’t a sustainable solution you see. Become a programmer, not some code monkey (though I think code monkey is a badge of honor, but you get my meaning). Programming is hard, everything you decide to do is hard. Becoming a plumber or electrician is hard. Takes years. But you can make a good living if you become good at this. Take the time it takes.

Question: I like to use Linux but I don't have any knowledge about Linux distro. Where should I start?

Watch videos on how to make a virtual machine on your computer, install those operating system as a virtual machine. Yes, do this, unless you have a 2nd machine. Then simply take one step at a time. Learn to configure it by watching videos and reading books. It will go very slowly at first. No matter how convenient it is, don’t use root as your user, just don’t. Just decide what you want to get out of using Linux. What goals do you need to accomplish in order to feel good about this experiment? Make a top 10 list of things you do on your computer today. Accomplish them on Linux. Once you have installed it, start to feel good about this. Don’t feel like you are using something complicated, it isn’t any more complicated than Windows, seriously, Windows is very complicated once you need to change the smallest details. It is fine watching videos with advanced Linux use, you are not there yet, you will get there. Just know that you can do those things using Linux, either write down notes (best) or try to make a mental note of it. You don’t need to know exactly every step, just know you can accomplish the thing that is being accomplished. Learn basic Linux. Read books, a lot of books are available for free, e-books. Buy used books at http://alibris.com or some other shop. Buy kindle books. Learn why user management is important (don’t become root), why sudo is your friend and what sudo is. (I think sudo means superuser do … something). You will not get this in few days. You will get this, like I said, it isn’t complicated. If you just want to be a user, GUI user, fine. Then don’t learn command line utilities. You can always learn it later, just keep in mind that a few things do require command line to do, but chances are that you don’t do those things in Windows today either, so it waits for another day. For browsing, editing text, even office work, Linux, out of the box, no command line is just fine. Libreoffice is actually very good office software, like really great. If you have a certain workflow or ideas in mind how windows works, don’t try to change Linux into Windows, you probably can get quite close. I also tell this to people who try a Mac, learn how it is supposed to be done on the device itself. Be it Linux or Mac, they have their way of working, Windows has that as well. Other apps and services on those platforms try to mimic how the operating system looks and feels to help you out. So, don’t just quit because everything isn’t just the way you think is better, like Windows is. You just have to learn how to do them in Linux. A short story of myself. I used Linux since it was in a beta version in 1991 or thereabout. Before the WWW became a thing. But mostly I used Windows and MS-DOS. In around 2003, I finally made enough money to buy a nice Mac Powerbook (that is what they were called back then). Everything was different, back then macOS X wasn’t even all that finished, 10.2. I mostly bought it because I had started to take digital photos and the JPEG virus had just been rampant, destroying everyone's JPG photos. I wanted a safe system and I was intrigued with Mac OS X. I decided to not try to use the same apps or tools and re-configure keyboard mapping and so on, like I still see many people do. I learnt to use a Mac the way it was expected. This also keeps a better separation between your computers. Set yourself this goal. For the next 10 days, everything you will do, will be done on Linux. Even the things that you have no idea how to do, especially them. Gaming and if someone is paying you to work differently is ok to go back for. But sending email, browsing, writing, note taking, photo handling and everything else, learn to use Linux. Don’t give up.
